keywords.def: angle of incidence in the denser medium for which the angle of refraction is 90 degrees
all light reflected inside the denser medium when the angle exceeds c
a medium with higher refractive index
thin glass strand that carries light by repeated total internal reflection

starter: Bismillah. State the equation for refractive index.
Calculate n for i = 30 and r = 19.5 degrees.
State what happens to the speed of light when it moves from glass to air.

teach.heading: What is the critical angle?
bullets: Light goes from glass (dense) towards air
Small i: light mostly refracts out
At i = c: refracted ray runs along the surface
Beyond c: total internal reflection
teach.note: Draw three rays: i less than c, i equal to c (angle of refraction 90 degrees), i greater than c (total internal reflection). A weak reflected ray is also seen at small angles. Total internal reflection needs two conditions: the light is travelling in the denser medium and i is greater than c.

head: Angle of incidence
What happens
rows: most light refracts out, a little reflects
refracted ray travels along the boundary

teach.heading: Experiment: semicircular block
bullets: Place the block with the flat face on a protractor
Aim the ray at the centre of the flat face along a radius
Increase i slowly from the curved side
Note i when the emerging ray vanishes along the surface
teach.note: Because the ray enters along the radius it is not bent at the curved face, so the angle at the flat face equals the angle on the protractor. Find c as the angle at which the refracted ray just disappears along the flat face. Repeat three times and take a mean. Safety: ray box lamps get hot, so do not touch.
cycle: Aim the ray at the flat face's centre
Start with a small angle of incidence
Increase i in steps
Record the angle when the refracted ray skims the surface
Repeat and take a mean

teach.heading: Link to refractive index
bullets: At i = c, r = 90 degrees
n = sin 90 / sin c = 1 / sin c
So sin c = 1 / n
Higher n gives a smaller critical angle
teach.note: Using n = sin i/sin r in reverse: for light leaving the material the roles swap. At the critical angle sin r = sin 90 = 1, giving sin c = 1/n.

model.problem: Glass has a refractive index of 1.50. Calculate its critical angle.

teach.heading: Check: total internal reflection
bullets: Whiteboards
teach.note: Option A is a typical error: TIR can't happen from air to glass. Option C confuses the critical angle with 90 degrees.

check.q: Light in glass hits the glass-air boundary at an angle greater than the critical angle. What happens?
options: it refracts out of the glass
it is totally reflected back into the glass
it speeds up in the glass
check.why: Above the critical angle there is no refracted ray, so all the light is totally internally reflected.

teach.heading: Where it is used
bullets: Optical fibres carry signals
Prisms in binoculars
Cat's-eye reflectors
Endoscopes in medicine
teach.note: Ask pupils to explain an optical fibre: light enters at a small angle to the axis so it hits the wall at an angle greater than c every time, so it is totally reflected and travels along the fibre with little loss.

Explain why total internal reflection cannot happen when light goes from air into glass.

Calculate c for n = 1.60.
Big question: when does light stop leaving the glass?

object that gives out radiation
object that takes in radiation

teach.heading: Units for energy and power
bullets: Energy and work: joule (J)
Power: watt (W) = J/s
Mass: kg; velocity: m/s; acceleration: m/s2
Force: N; distance: m; time: s
teach.note: Include a quick calculation to link the units: a 2.0 kg trolley at 3.0 m/s has KE = 0.5 x 2.0 x 3.0 squared = 9.0 J. Work done = force x distance, so N x m = J. Power = energy / time, so J/s = W. Ask pupils to track units through each step.

teach.heading: Convection in everyday life
bullets: Warm fluid expands and becomes less dense
It rises; cooler, denser fluid sinks
A convection current is set up
Examples: sea breeze, radiators, kettles, boilers
teach.note: Only in fluids (liquids and gases), not solids. Sea breeze: the land heats faster than the sea in the day, warm air rises over land, cooler air from the sea moves in. At night the pattern reverses. Immersion heaters are placed near the bottom of a tank so the warm water rises. Freezer compartments are at the top of a fridge so cold air sinks. Hot-air balloons rise because heated air is less dense.

It becomes less dense and rises
Cooler, denser fluid sinks to replace it
The fluid is heated again
A convection current keeps flowing

teach.heading: Worked example: explain a sea breeze
bullets: Link land heating to density
Name the movement of air
Complete the circuit of air
teach.note: Pupils lose marks for saying 'heat rises'; the accurate statement is that warm air is less dense and rises.

model.problem: Explain why a sea breeze blows from the sea to the land on a hot afternoon.
steps: The land heats up faster than the sea
Air above the land is heated, expands and becomes less dense
Cooler, denser air from the sea flows in to replace it

teach.heading: Check: radiators

check.q: Why is a room heated by a radiator warmed throughout?
options: the radiator conducts heat through the air
warm air rises and sets up a convection current
cold air rises and moves away
check.why: Air next to the radiator warms, becomes less dense and rises. Cooler air moves in, setting up a convection current.

teach.heading: Emitting and absorbing radiation
bullets: All objects emit infrared radiation
Hotter objects emit more radiation
Dark, matt surfaces: good emitters and absorbers
Light, shiny surfaces: poor emitters and absorbers
teach.note: Leslie cube: four faces (matt black, shiny black, matt white, shiny silver) at the same temperature; an infrared detector shows the matt black face emits most. Solar panels and radiator surfaces are dark and matt; emergency blankets and fire-fighter suits are shiny so they reflect radiation; houses in hot places are often painted white. Ask: why are the back of a fridge's pipes black and matt?

teach.heading: Temperature matters too
bullets: Higher temperature: more radiation per second
The surface of the Sun emits a lot
An object at room temperature emits infrared
Equal absorbing and emitting means constant temperature
teach.note: Link to the Earth: when the rate of absorbing equals the rate of emitting, the temperature stays constant; if absorption rises, the temperature goes up. Keep the idea qualitative.
